paragraphs: Historians of ordinary life depend on records, and records are produced by institutions with purposes of their own. Tax rolls, court registers and parish books were kept to collect, to punish and to enroll, not to describe how people lived, and those who left no mark in them, such as the landless poor and the unlettered, are therefore easy to overlook. It is tempting to conclude that such people simply did not matter to the societies whose records omit them.

That inference is mistaken. The scarcity of references to the landless poor is itself informative, and so are the occasions on which they do appear, as defendants, as recipients of charity, as the subject of a neighbor's complaint, for these entries reveal what the authorities feared or tolerated. A historian who reads such entries against the grain, asking why a clerk troubled to write them down, can recover traces of lives that the record was never designed to keep. The method is laborious and its results are partial, but it restores voices that the archive has otherwise muffled.
